thread.title: Why I Am Buying Apple - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: PendragonY
title: Why I Am Buying Apple - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Figure 1 Historic Apple Logo
What did I think last time? I last wrote about Apple ( AAPL ) back at the end of July last year. At the time I thought it was a bit over-valued but that for those who had the time to wait for its growth to play out that it could be a good investment anyway. My thinking was that a great company at a fair price is a good investment and that Apple is clearly a great company.
Figure 2 July 2017 DDM calculation
Back in July I thought the dividend stream for Apple, for those with more than 10 years to go until retirement, was around $150. With the market price just under $156 I thought that was a reasonable premium to pay for such a great company. I got a lot of push back from folks who thought I was being far too negative about Apple’s prospects.
What new information do we have now? I was reading the other day about how Apple made more profit in the first 3 months of this year than Amazon has made in its entire existence. Apple’s net income for the March quarter of 2018 was $13.8 billion while Amazon’s total net income since it began has only been $9.6 billion. To me that is a truly great company. I want to own great companies and, even more, I want to own great companies that generate so much cash that they can send some of it to me (and if they really have to the other shareholders too). That very much describes Apple.
As a dividend growth investor, I like dividend increases . I really liked the 10 cent a quarter hike that Apple announced on May 1 of this year. I like it even better since this increase produces a yearly dividend that in 12 cents higher than the $2.80 I predicted in my last article.
Looking at the earnings reports , the May 1 report is the latest in a series of earnings beats. May 1 was the 8 th quarter in a row where Apple beat EPS expectations, and the 7 th time (over this time frame) where it beat revenue expectations. That says solid consistent growth, a mark of a great company in my opinion.
The iPhone is critical to Apple’s success. So news that the iPhone X is once again the most popular cell phone, selling 16 million units, is very good for Apple. And it’s even better that the next 3 spots on the list are also iPhones. In order for Apple to pay me the future dividends I will want if I own it, revenues (and profits too) will need to grow fairly dramatically. The continued dominance of the iPhone will be required to deliver that revenue growth. It’s possible that in the future, some other product of Apple’s will be able to deliver that revenue and profit growth, but at this point I don’t see such a product.
As a dividend growth investor I like to read article by other dividend growth investors on what they think about stocks I am interested in owning. So I read this article by Robert Kovacs. Robert makes the case that while Apple is a great company, given his goals for current income Apple isn’t a suitable investment for him. I have no problems with Robert’s assessment or with applying that assessment to folks whose biggest needs are current income. But for those dividend growth investors that don’t need more income now and have at least 10 years to wait for Apple to grow, I think Apple is a great investment choice.
What’s a good price? To figure out a good price, I do a DDM calculation using my Excel based DDM calculator (pictured below, you can see the web-based calculator I based it on here and read a discussion on how the formulas were developed here ). I also found this discussion of DDM, and note that in the article the author uses a discount rate of 5%.
Looking at the David Fish’s CCC List (which contains data on companies that have raised their dividend each year for 5 or more years) I see that Apple has increased the dividend each year for 6 years. That is on the shorter side, but Apple also has tons of cash (that might not be literal but it isn’t far off from being literal) and is accumulating more. The payout ratio is also quite low, so I am confident that Apple can increase the dividend even faster than it has been if management so desired. I want to buy shares in companies that generate so much cash that they can afford to send some of it to me, and Apple is generating so much cash that not only is it the best use of some of it to send it to me, that it can’t find enough uses for it that it builds up like dust bunnies under the bed.
So, much as I did in the last article, I will assume that over the next 12 months I will collect the currently declared dividend 4 times, giving me a total dividend payment of $2.92.
Figure 3 https://finviz.com/quote.ashx?t=AAPL
The table above is from finviz.com and shows some valuation metrics as well as analysts’ growth projections for Apple. For me, in trying to determine what dividend growth I can expect, the most important number is the expected growth in EPS over the next 5 years. I think that the 13.45% expected growth in EPS is more than enough to support the 11.1% growth in the estimated dividend. Because Apple is still a growth company, I will also expect the dividend growth to be sustainable out to 10 years instead of the usual 5 years.
Some may point out that not many companies grow the dividend that fast every year for 10 years, but I don’t need Apple to actually do that every year. It can, and will, grow the dividend faster than 11% (like it did this year), so that in those years where the dividend grows at a slower rate, the CAGR over the whole period will still average out to be 11.1%.
Figure 4 DDM for May 2018
Using those parameters sets my buy price at $173. With Apple closing Monday at $188.15, that buy price would say that Apple is too expensive. But is it? I think it very much depends on individual goals and expectations.
Back last July, I was willing to pay a premium for Apple and even pay as much at $156 (a 4% premium to the NPV of the dividends). How would that have worked out for me? Well, the shares I paid $156 for are now selling for $188 or about 20% more. Over the first 12 months I owned the shares I expected to collect $2.52 in dividends but will now collect $2.62. And in all likelihood the dividends collected even farther out in time will be higher than I expected. I didn’t end up buying those shares, but that was because I saw what I thought was better value elsewhere. I now think that I underestimated the value of the Apple shares.
Right now, my portfolio is well on track to exceed my income goals for the year. So far the dividends I have collected are 17.8% ahead of the amount collected by the same date last year, when I only need 12% income growth. So I am in a good position to add shares for future growth rather than current income.
So let’s look at what the dividend stream might be worth in 2 years’ time if my growth assumptions for Apple prove to be correct. The projected next 12 months of dividend payments could be $3.60. Keeping the other parameters the same, I can see what I might be willing to pay for Apple 2 years down the road.
Figure 5 May 2020 DDM calculation
So in May of 2020, if my assumptions about Apple’s growth prove to be correct (and even more so if my expectations are exceeded), I would be willing to buy shares of Apple at any price under $215. So how much would I need to set aside now so that in 2020 I have that $215 to buy the Apple shares? I can just discount that amount back, much like I discount the value of future dividends, for the 2 years I will wait to I need it. That makes the amount of cash I need now just $189.
Now, I can certainly keep the $189 invested in my portfolio, and I have every confidence that I will have the $215 in 2020 when I need it to buy shares of Apple. But, there is still a risk to that strategy. I didn’t buy Apple at $156 when I had the chance, and now it is at $188. So what happens if Apple is higher than $215 in 2020? Right now, Apple is trading at $188. So what happens if I buy Apple now, since it is below the $189 I need to set aside to buy Apple in 2 years? Well, if Apple is at $215 or higher, than I am quite happy. If Apple is below $215, I am still fairly happy as long as it is above $189. And I have more than $6 per share in dividend payments to console me.
Once again, because I think this is a very important point, because I have my current income needs met, I can afford to add some shares where future growth is the priority instead of current income. Apple makes sense only in that context. And Apple makes sense only if you can afford to wait 10 or more years for that growth to play out. If, and only if, those conditions apply to you and your investments is Apple a good buy.
What to watch for going forward? Going forward I think the state of the legal battles with Qualcomm ( QCOM ) are the most important thing to keep an eye on. About 2 weeks ago, Qualcomm announced some concessions in the hopes of ending the battle. Two provisions I think are very important to Apple. First, I think the inclusion of the 5G patents with no additional cost is of great benefit to Apple. They offer premium phones at a premium price and so having no extra licensing cost to them of being able to include 5G in their phones is a big deal. I think the second provision, where fees will be charged on only the first $400 of the phone price, is an even bigger deal for Apple.
Apple’s main complaint has been that isn’t fair that they have to pay more for a license if it’s on a more expensive phone. Their argument centered around it being unfair that someone else got the benefit of their work. It is now apparent that to some extent they were not paying more and with the new provision even more of Apple’s higher end phones will be at the cap in license fees. The new provision, and the old one too, both addresses Apple’s chief complaint and undermines it.
Conclusion Apple is a great company that is both a growth company and a dividend growth company. While current yield is still on the low end, for those dividend growth investors who have the time to wait for growth, that isn’t a big problem. I really wish I had bought some shares back last July. But I think there is still a good opportunity for me to buy shares now. I plan to do so as soon as I have the cash to buy shares. I should have that cash by the end of the month.
Note: I hope you all got something out of this article. I do appreciate the time you took reading it. If you are one of those who follow me here, I appreciate it; if you'd like to include yourself amongst those individuals, please hit the "Follow" button next to my name as well as following other contributors whose work you enjoy. Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
